cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Can a thief give a bona fide buyer ownership of the stolen thing?
cards.old_front: Kann ein Dieb dem gutgläubigen Käufer Eigentum an der gestohlenen Sache verschaffen?
cards.back:
No — NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET: the thief has only possession, not ownership, and therefore cannot transfer any.
• Through the delivery (TRADITIO) the buyer acquires only possession, derivatively; since he possesses on the basis of a sale (IUSTA CAUSA), he has civil possession.
• Usucaption (USUCAPIO) also fails: the thing is a RES FURTIVA — under the LEX ATINIA it cannot be usucapted even by later acquirers in good faith.
• The victim of the theft remains owner and can proceed against any possessor with the REI VINDICATIO (Example 1: Clara against Leander).

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is a RES FURTIVA and what consequence does it have for USUCAPIO?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine RES FURTIVA und welche Folge hat sie für die USUCAPIO?
cards.back:
A stolen movable thing — it cannot be usucapted (LEX ATINIA).
• FURTUM = taking another's movable thing with intent to enrich oneself; it also covers embezzlement (a depositary sells the thing entrusted to him) and keeping a thing that has obviously been lost.
• The bar on usucaption affects the thief AND all later acquirers, whether in good or bad faith — the blemish attaches to the thing.
• It only ceases when the thing returns into the owner's power (REVERSIO IN POTESTATEM).
• Land cannot be stolen; a similar bar applies to land seized by force (LEGES IULIAE ET PLAUTIAE).

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Which actions does the victim of a theft have — against the thief and against a third party who possesses the thing?
cards.old_front: Welche Klagen hat der Bestohlene — gegen den Dieb und gegen einen Dritten, der die Sache besitzt?
cards.back:
Against the thief: ACTIO FURTI (penal action for a penalty) + CONDICTIO FURTIVA (for the thing or its value) — cumulative.
• Against any possessor, including a third-party acquirer in good faith: REI VINDICATIO (ACTIO IN REM) — but only as long as the thing exists.
• The CONDICTIO FURTIVA lies only against the thief himself (not an ACTIO IN REM), but it also applies if he no longer has the thing or it has perished.
• CONDICTIO FURTIVA and REI VINDICATIO both pursue the thing → not cumulative; the owner must choose.
• Possessory interdicts only against someone whose possession is flawed in relation to him (the thief: CLAM) — not against the third-party acquirer (Example 1: Leander).

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: When does the transfer of possession (TRADITIO) also transfer ownership — brief overview for the possession cases?
cards.old_front: Wann überträgt die Besitzübergabe (TRADITIO) zugleich das Eigentum — Kurzüberblick für die Besitzfälle?
cards.back:
When the transferor is owner (or has authority of disposal) and there is a valid legal ground for acquisition (IUSTA CAUSA) — e.g. sale, gift, loan, dowry (DOS).
• TRADITIO = transfer of possession, also by TRADITIO BREVI MANU or CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM.
• The sale alone transfers neither possession nor ownership.
• RES NEC MANCIPI (e.g. wine, vase, carriage): the acquirer becomes civil-law owner.
• RES MANCIPI (Italic land, slaves, cattle, horses, donkeys, mules): mere TRADITIO gives only bonitarian ownership; civil-law ownership only through MANCIPATIO/IN IURE CESSIO or once the usucaption period has elapsed.

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Are gifts between spouses valid in Roman law?
cards.old_front: Sind Schenkungen zwischen Ehegatten im römischen Recht gültig?
cards.back:
No — from early times Roman law has prohibited gifts between spouses; they are void.
• That is why Ulpian D 6.1.77 (Case 20) expressly stresses that the donee is NOT the donor's husband.
• Example 18: Aulus cannot gratuitously convey his garden to his wife Aurelia during his lifetime.
• The prohibition is IUS COGENS — it cannot be excluded by agreement.

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is a LOCATIO CONDUCTIO — and what possessory position does the tenant or usufructuary lessee have?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine LOCATIO CONDUCTIO — und welche Besitzstellung hat der Mieter oder Pächter?
cards.back:
LOCATIO CONDUCTIO = contract of lease (lease agreement): letting a thing for use in return for payment; in a usufructuary lease also for taking its fruits.
• Tenants and usufructuary lessees (CONDUCTOR, COLONUS) are detentors: they hold the thing with ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI for the lessor, who remains mediate proprietary possessor (Example 4: Rusticus leases his field to Lea).
• Sub-lease → chain of detentors; it does not harm the lessor's possession.
• Only contractual claims (ACTIONES IN PERSONAM), no right in rem — e.g. the lessee's ACTIO CONDUCTI against the lessor.
• Contract for work (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS): the customer supplies the material and remains owner of the finished work.

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Is the transfer of possession (TRADITIO) a legal act — does the transferor lose possession if the recipient does not acquire it?
cards.old_front: Ist die Besitzübertragung (TRADITIO) ein Rechtsgeschäft — verliert der Übergebende den Besitz, wenn der Empfänger keinen Besitz erwirbt?
cards.back:
Disputed.
• Ulpian D 41.2.34 pr (Case 44) and others: No — TRADITIO is a legal act; the transferor intends to give up possession only on condition that the other party acquires it. If the latter does not acquire it (e.g. for lack of capacity to act), the transferor remains possessor.
• Celsus D 41.2.18.1 (Case 43): the transferor gives up possession in any event; if the recipient does not acquire it, the thing is without a possessor.
• Background: the law seeks to preserve existing possessory situations as far as possible (cf. Ex 4b: Merops is asleep and does not acquire possession).

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is a RATIHABITIO — how does it operate in the acquisition of possession through persons in power?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine RATIHABITIO — wie wirkt sie beim Besitzerwerb durch Gewaltunterworfene?
cards.back:
Subsequent ratification by the DOMINUS — it is treated as if he had given an IUSSUM beforehand.
• RATI ENIM HABITIO MANDATO COMPARATUR — subsequent ratification is equivalent to an authorisation (Ulpian D 46.3.12.4).
• Significance: without an IUSSUM and without a PECULIUM the DOMINUS does not acquire possession through the person in his power; the RATIHABITIO supplies the missing ANIMUS afterwards.
• With a PECULIUM it is unnecessary — there a general authorisation already exists.

cards.topic: 27.10. Acquiring ownership I — TRADITIO
cards.front: What is a loan (MUTUUM) — and how does it differ from a gift (DONATIO)?
cards.old_front: Was ist ein Darlehen (MUTUUM) — und wie unterscheidet es sich von der Schenkung (DONATIO)?
cards.back:
MUTUUM = loan for consumption: the lender transfers ownership to the recipient, usually of money; the recipient is obliged to repay the sum in the future.
• In common with a gift: transfer of ownership without consideration. Difference: gift = permanent, loan = only temporary.
• Both are an IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS (alongside sale and dowry).
• Both come into existence only with delivery between consenting parties — no prior agreement needed.
• Dissent gift/loan → controversy Julian D 41.1.36 vs Ulpian D 12.1.18 pr.

cards.topic: 27.10. Acquiring ownership I — TRADITIO
cards.front: How does the recipient acquire another's money ORIGINALLY — and why does this matter where a TRADITIO has failed?
cards.old_front: Wie erwirbt der Empfänger fremdes Geld ORIGINÄR — und warum ist das bei einer gescheiterten TRADITIO wichtig?
cards.back:
By “consuming” the coins (NUMMOS CONSUMERE): above all by mixing them indistinguishably with his own money or by spending them in good faith.
• Until then the transferor remains owner → REI VINDICATIO as long as the coins are present and distinguishable.
• Afterwards vindication is excluded; the transferor is left only with the CONDICTIO (unjust enrichment for lack of a causa).
• Application: Ulpian D 12.1.18 pr (Case 71) — for lack of an IUSTA CAUSA no derivative acquisition; only consumption makes D owner by original acquisition.

cards.topic: 27.10. Acquiring ownership I — TRADITIO
cards.front: What is the EXCEPTIO DOLI (plea of fraud) — how can it defeat an owner's REI VINDICATIO?
cards.old_front: Was ist die EXCEPTIO DOLI (Einrede der Arglist) — wie kann sie eine REI VINDICATIO des Eigentümers abwehren?
cards.back:
A plea (EXCEPTIO) of the defendant: the plaintiff is formally entitled (e.g. still owner), but his action would be fraudulent — it is then dismissed.
• Typical case: VENIRE CONTRA FACTUM PROPRIUM — the owner reclaims what he himself wanted to give away.
• Iavolenus D 39.5.25 (Case 68): E remains owner, but Titius may keep the gift by means of the EXCEPTIO DOLI (BENIGNIUS EST).
• Ulpian D 12.1.18 pr (Case 71): C wanted to make a gift → his REI VINDICATIO or CONDICTIO fails because of the EXCEPTIO DOLI.

cards.topic: 27.10. Acquiring ownership I — Overview of the modes of acquisition
cards.front: What is a USUSFRUCTUS (usufruct) — and does it survive if the owner alienates the thing?
cards.old_front: Was ist ein USUSFRUCTUS (Nießbrauch) — und bleibt er bestehen, wenn der Eigentümer die Sache veräußert?
cards.back:
A right in rem to use another's thing and take its fruits without altering its substance: USUSFRUCTUS EST IUS ALIENIS REBUS UTENDI FRUENDI SALVA RERUM SUBSTANTIA (Paulus D 7.1.1).
• Personal servitude — tied to the person, it is extinguished on that person's death.
• The usufructuary may use the thing but not sell it (Example 2: Laura).
• Alienation: the acquirer becomes owner, but encumbered with the usufruct — NEMO PLUS IURIS … (Example 21: Leo conveys the slave woman Pomona to Ajax by MANCIPATIO, Verres keeps the USUSFRUCTUS).
• Usually created by legacy (providing e.g. for the wife without making her heir).

cards.topic: 27.10. Acquiring ownership I — Overview of the modes of acquisition
cards.front: What legal position does the heir (HERES) acquire in the deceased's things — can he have more rights than the deceased?
cards.old_front: Welche Rechtsstellung erwirbt der Erbe (HERES) an den Sachen des Erblassers — kann er mehr Rechte haben als dieser?
cards.back:
No — the heir steps into the deceased's legal position: he receives the deceased's rights as they were and also takes over the deceased's debts.
• If the deceased had a thing only on deposit (or on loan, or on lease), the heir does not inherit ownership and cannot transfer any either (NEMO PLUS IURIS …).
• If the deceased owned only a share in joint ownership, only that share passes.
• The heir continues a usucaption begun by the deceased (SUCCESSIO IN POSSESSIONEM) — his own good faith is not required.

cards.topic: 03.11. Acquiring ownership II — LEX ATINIA and REVERSIO IN POTESTATEM
cards.front: Can an owner commit FURTUM of his own thing — e.g. the pledger against the pledgee?
cards.old_front: Kann der Eigentümer an seiner eigenen Sache FURTUM begehen — zB der Verpfänder gegenüber dem Pfandgläubiger?
cards.back:
Yes — whoever takes away his own thing, which he has handed over to the pledgee, without the latter's permission is liable to him as a FUR (Paulus (Cassius) D 41.3.4.21, Case 74).
• Background on pledge (PIGNUS): the pledger hands over his thing to the creditor as security for a claim; the pledgee has a limited right in rem and (natural) possession protected by interdicts.
• Likewise a FUR is a pledger who knowingly alienates a movable pledged thing without the creditor's consent (Paulus (Iulianus) D 47.2.67 pr).
• Whether the thing thereby remains a RES FURTIVA or becomes capable of usucaption as soon as it returns to the owner is disputed (Case 74 vs Labeo D 41.3.49, Case 75).

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — Formulary procedure (IN IURE / APUD IUDICEM)
cards.front: What is an ACTIO UTILIS — and how does it relate to the ACTIO IN FACTUM?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine ACTIO UTILIS — und wie verhält sie sich zur ACTIO IN FACTUM?
cards.back:
An action granted by the praetor by analogy: he takes an action of the edict as a model (EXEMPLUM) and extends it to a case not covered by its wording.
• Like the ACTIO IN FACTUM, an action for a legitimate claim where no suitable action of the edict exists; the formula of the ACTIO IN FACTUM begins with a description of the concrete facts.
• Examples: action of the owner of the panel against the painter (TABULA PICTA, Gaius Inst 2.78); REI VINDICATIO UTILIS of the emphyteuta; ACTIO PIGNERATICIA (IN REM) UTILIS on convalescence of the pledge; ACTIO UTILIS of lower-ranking pledgees for their share of the SUPERFLUUM.

cards.topic: 17.11. Acquiring ownership III — ACCESSIO
cards.front: What is the ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM — what is it for?
cards.old_front: Was ist die ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM — wozu dient sie?
cards.back:
An action that compels the production (EXHIBITIO) or separation of a thing and thus prepares the REI VINDICATIO.
• Where things are joined separably (e.g. an arm attached by soldering — ADPLUMBATIO; parts screwed on) it is used to obtain separation; afterwards each owner vindicates his thing.
• Not necessary for mixing (immediate VINDICATIO PRO PARTE); not admissible for building a house (no separation of building materials).
• Its formula also covers anyone who has fraudulently ceased to possess (QUI DOLO DESIIT POSSIDERE).

cards.topic: 17.11. Acquiring ownership III — ACCESSIO
cards.front: What do FERRUMINATIO and ADPLUMBATIO mean — what consequence does each have for ownership?
cards.old_front: Was bedeuten FERRUMINATIO und ADPLUMBATIO — welche Folge hat jede für das Eigentum?
cards.back:
FERRUMINATIO = welding: inseparable joining → the owner of the principal thing acquires the welded-on part (ACCESSIO CEDIT PRINCIPALI); the former owner has the ACTIO IN FACTUM for compensation.
ADPLUMBATIO = soldering: separable joining (the solder separates the metal parts) → no change of ownership; ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM, then REI VINDICATIO.
• Paulus D 6.1.23.5 (Case 113): F's metal arm on E's statue.
• If the welded-on part later breaks off, it remains the property of the owner of the principal thing — the former right has been extinguished for good.

cards.topic: 17.11. Acquiring ownership III — ACCESSIO
cards.front: TABULA PICTA: Why does the high classical view treat painting on another's wooden panel differently from writing on another's paper?
cards.old_front: TABULA PICTA: Warum behandelt die hochklassische Meinung das Bemalen einer fremden Holztafel anders als das Beschreiben fremden Papiers?
cards.back:
Because the painter's artistic achievement is to take precedence — under the view prevailing in Gaius' time the picture exceptionally belongs to the painter.
• Otherwise the rule is: the principal thing is what can be vindicated independently → writing on another's paper/parchment belongs to the owner of the paper (Gaius D 41.1.9.1).
• Compensation: the former owner of the panel has an ACTIO UTILIS; the painter asserts his costs by EXCEPTIO DOLI.
• Gaius himself rejects the exception; in late classical law the uniform rule is: the picture belongs to the owner of the panel (Paulus D 6.1.23.3).

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — REI VINDICATIO
cards.front: What does FACULTAS RESTITUENDI mean — who, on that basis, can be sued with the REI VINDICATIO?
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet FACULTAS RESTITUENDI — wer kann danach mit der REI VINDICATIO beklagt werden?
cards.back:
The factual ability to return the disputed thing to the plaintiff.
• Ulpian (late classical, D 6.1.9): anyone who can return the thing can be sued — including natural possessors without interdict protection.
• Pegasus (early classical): only those with possession protected by interdicts — proprietary possessors and natural possessors protected by interdicts (e.g. pledgee, precarist).
• No possession, no condemnation — except for FICTI POSSESSORES (PRO POSSESSIONE DOLUS EST).

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — REI VINDICATIO
cards.front: What does CULPA IN ELIGENDO mean?
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet CULPA IN ELIGENDO?
cards.back:
Fault in choosing assistants: whoever entrusts a thing to less suitable persons acts negligently and is liable for its loss.
• Paulus D 6.1.16.1 (Case 126): the defendant who, after the LITIS CONTESTATIO, sends the vindicated ship to sea during the sailing season is not liable for its loss — but he is if he entrusts it to “less suitable persons”.
• Background: in the Sabinian view the defendant is liable after the LITIS CONTESTATIO for DOLUS and CULPA.

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — REI VINDICATIO
cards.front: What is an ARGUMENTUM A MINORE AD MAIUS?
cards.old_front: Was ist ein ARGUMENTUM A MINORE AD MAIUS?
cards.back:
An inference from the lesser to the greater: if even the weaker requirement triggers the legal consequence, then all the more so the stronger one.
• Example: if the defendant in a REI VINDICATIO is liable even for negligence (CULPA), then all the more so for intent (DOLUS) (textbook on Paulus D 6.1.16.1, Case 126).

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — REI VINDICATIO
cards.front: What role does the LEX AQUILIA play in the protection of ownership?
cards.old_front: Welche Rolle spielt die LEX AQUILIA beim Schutz des Eigentums?
cards.back:
It is the basis of the Roman law of damages for the unlawful and culpable destruction of (or damage to) another's things.
• If the defendant culpably destroys the disputed thing already BEFORE the LITIS CONTESTATIO, the REI VINDICATIO fails (neither possession nor thing) — but the owner can claim compensation under the LEX AQUILIA.
• The Sabinian liability after the LITIS CONTESTATIO for DOLUS and CULPA corresponds to the delictual liability of the LEX AQUILIA.

cards.topic: 17.11. Protection of ownership — ACTIO PUBLICIANA, pleas, ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: What does convalescence mean — when is an acquisition from an unauthorised person cured retrospectively?
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet Konvaleszenz — wann wird der Erwerb vom Nichtberechtigten nachträglich geheilt?
cards.back:
Convalescence = retroactive curing of a legal defect: if the unauthorised transferor subsequently acquires ownership (e.g. by inheritance), the acquirer is placed as if he had acquired from the owner.
• Pomponius (Iulianus) D 21.3.2 (Case 130): T buys land belonging to S from Titius; Titius becomes S's heir → T becomes bonitarian owner, Titius keeps only the NUDUM IUS QUIRITIUM.
• If Titius then alienates the land a second time, he can no longer give the second acquirer anything (NEMO PLUS IURIS …) → T prevails with the ACTIO PUBLICIANA.
• The same idea applies to a pledge of another's thing: if the pledger later becomes owner, the pledge convalesces (ACTIO PIGNERATICIA (IN REM) UTILIS).

cards.topic: 01.12. Pledge II — Blanket liens, aggregates, tacit liens
cards.front: What is an aggregate of things (UNIVERSITAS RERUM) — and how does a pledge over it operate (e.g. over a TABERNA)?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine Sachgesamtheit (UNIVERSITAS RERUM) — und wie wirkt ein Pfandrecht an ihr (zB an einer TABERNA)?
cards.back:
Physically separate things that form an economic unit and are treated as one thing in property law (e.g. shop/TABERNA, herd) — they can be sold, pledged and sued for as a whole.
• Pledge over a changing stock: each item becomes pledged as soon as the pledger acquires ownership of it and it comes into the shop — even after processing, as long as it stays there.
• Once it leaves the shop, the pledge over it is extinguished (the creditor is presumed to have consented to the alienation = waiver).
• Only things belonging to the pledger are covered (Scaevola D 20.1.34 pr, Case 159b).

cards.topic: 01.12. Pledge II — Multiple liens and priority
cards.front: What is a potestative condition — and what rank does a pledge securing a conditional claim have?
cards.old_front: Was ist eine Potestativbedingung — und welchen Rang hat ein Pfandrecht, das eine bedingte Forderung sichert?
cards.back:
Potestative condition = a condition whose fulfilment lies at the debtor's discretion.
• Africanus D 20.4.9.1 (Case 177): a pledge created earlier for a conditional claim ranks ahead of a later one for an unconditional claim — except in the case of a potestative condition.
• If the condition fails, the pledge is extinguished (accessoriness).
• To be distinguished: the conditional pledge as a preliminary stage of a subsequent pledge — the second creditor receives the pledge on condition that the first one is extinguished; if the first creditor enforces his pledge, it never comes into existence.

cards.topic: 01.12. Pledge II — Multiple liens and priority
cards.front: What is the CRIMEN STELLIONATUS in the law of pledge?
cards.old_front: Was ist das CRIMEN STELLIONATUS im Pfandrecht?
cards.back:
The criminal liability of a debtor who fraudulently conceals from the pledgee existing pledges over the pledged thing.
• The duty to inform about other pledges is an ancillary duty arising from the contract of pledge.
• Relevant in multiple pledging, e.g. when the surplus (HYPEROCHA = SUPERFLUUM) is pledged to a second creditor (Tryphoninus D 20.4.20, Case 172).
